(employing amicus briefs and the records of adjudicatory hearings applying the 
rule to discern the agency’s ‘"basis and purpose”). However, the jurisprudence 
is not uniform, and agencies would not be wise to count on judicial leniency. 
Many cases reject the use of any agency-generated explanations put forward 
in support of a rule, but subsequent to its issuance, as “post hoc 
rationalizations,” see Tabor v. Joint Bd. for Enrollment of Actuaries, 566 F.2d 
705 (D.C. Cir. 1977); Rodway v. USDA, 514 F.2d 809 (D.C. Cir. 1975), and 
refuse to parse the record for supporting data not relied upon in the agency’s 
contemporaneous rationale. See, e.g., Kennecott Copper Corp. v. EPA, 462 F.2d 
846 (D.C. Cir. 1972). The concerns reflected in such rulings seem to include (1) 
a desire to provide information to potential htigants who, if well-informed, 
might pursue further administrative procedures (such as a request for 
rehearing) rather than judicial review; (2) a desire to force agencies to be more 
exphcitly rational in justifying their choices, thereby (presumably) guarding 
against unknown influences that might have corrupted the administrative 
process; and (3) a desire to force reconsideration of superficially implausible 
decisions.

The Evolution of Informal Rulemaking. For many years the 
procedural requirements and judicial review standards of the APA were

“on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing,” the substantial 
evidence standard applied; when an agency could proceed informally—^in

the “arbitrary and capricious” standard. But the nexus between agency
